strengths: Introduces CULTIVate, a large benchmark for evaluating T2I models on culturally grounded social activities across 16 countries, 576 prompts, and over 19k generated images, filling a gap left by object-centric cultural benchmarks.

Proposes interpretable, automatic descriptor-based AHEaD metrics (Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, Diversity) using a proposer-refiner pipeline and MLLM descriptor extraction, enabling scalable cultural evaluation without human annotations.

Human study shows that the proposed metrics, especially the combined FAITH score, correlate more strongly with human cultural faithfulness judgments than existing image-text alignment metrics and MLLM judges.
Provides systematic evidence of Global North vs. Global South bias across six recent T2I models, with consistent gaps in alignment, hallucination, exaggeration, and diversity.
Ablations on the proposer-refiner pipeline and similarity threshold tau support key design choices, and human validation indicates ~90% relevance for generated descriptors.
weaknesses: Human evaluation is limited to 7 countries, 9 activities, 3 public models, and 216 forms, leaving proprietary models and most benchmark countries unvalidated; this weakens claims about metric effectiveness and broad cultural bias.

The composite FAITH metric is an unweighted arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, and 1-EXAG; because HAL values are high (~0.5) and EXAG values are low (~0.05), FAITH is dominated by 1-HAL and may not adequately reflect cultural alignment.

The Exaggeration metric depends on an underspecified LLM-generated stereotype candidate set and noisy real-image averages; Table 7 shows EXAG overall correlation (0.26) is lower than QwenVL (0.29), contradicting the claim that it achieves the highest correlation.

The Hallucination metric flags any predicted descriptor whose maximum similarity to ground-truth descriptors is below tau, which can conflate incompleteness or ambiguity in LLM-generated ground-truth descriptors with genuinely incorrect cultural elements.
Diversity metrics (DDIV and SDIV) are not validated against human judgments, and the semantic diversity definition may reward rare descriptor coverage rather than meaningful cultural variation.

Several central claims are overstated or inconsistent: the abstract/intro claim of '7% better correlation' is not clearly supported by Table 2, where FAITH overall (0.38) remains below human-human agreement (0.42), and Table 7 overclaims EXAG performance.

Benchmark construction relies on GPT-4o parsing of CulturalAtlas/Wikipedia and Google-searched real images filtered by CLIPScore, without expert cultural validation of all descriptors or references, risking LLM and web biases.

Reproducibility is unclear: the paper does not explicitly state whether the dataset, prompts, and code will be released, and proprietary model evaluations use N=1 due to cost, limiting comparability and replication.

Presentation quality suffers from inconsistent acronyms (AHEaD/AHEAD/CULTIVate/CULTIVATE), typos, unclear equations, and confusing table/caption descriptions, making some technical details hard to verify.

strengths: Tackles an important and understudied problem: cultural evaluation of text-to-image models for social activities, beyond object-centric categories.
Introduces a large-scale benchmark (CULTIVate) covering 16 countries, 9 activity categories, 576 prompts, over 19k generated images, and ~3k real reference images.

Proposes interpretable descriptor-based metrics (AHEaD) and shows that the combined faithfulness metric correlates more strongly with human judgments than several prior image-text alignment metrics (e.g., CLIPScore, VQAScore, PickScore).
Conducts a human evaluation with quality-control measures such as nationality/residence constraints, attention checks, repeated questions, and free-text rationales, and reports human-human agreement.
Provides a systematic analysis of Global North vs. Global South bias across multiple T2I models, revealing consistent disparities on social activities.
weaknesses: The central claim that AHEaD achieves '7% better correlation' is inconsistent with Table 2, where FAITH (0.38) vs. VQAScore (0.22) corresponds to a ~16 percentage point absolute or ~73% relative improvement, not 7%. This overclaim appears in the abstract and introduction.

The diversity metrics (DDIV, SDIV) are not validated against human judgments. The paper does not collect human ratings of diversity, yet claims these metrics capture cultural variation, leaving a core contribution unsubstantiated.

The exaggeration metric relies on an LLM-generated stereotype candidate set S_r, but the generation, filtering, and validation of this set are not described in sufficient detail. This introduces potential LLM bias into the metric.

The hallucination metric treats any predicted descriptor not in the GT descriptor set as a hallucination, which penalizes valid but unlisted cultural elements and conflates descriptor-set incompleteness with actual hallucination.

Real reference images are selected via CLIPScore filtering, even though the paper criticizes CLIPScore for cultural bias and bag-of-words behavior. This undermines the calibration and exaggeration metrics that depend on these references.
The Faithfulness metric is an ad hoc arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, and 1-EXAG without justification, learned weights, or comparison to alternative aggregation functions.

Human evaluation covers only 7 countries, 3 public models, and 189 images, while the benchmark spans 16 countries and 6 models. The validation does not support claims about the full benchmark or proprietary models.
No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported for the correlations, making it difficult to assess whether observed improvements are reliable.
No code or dataset release statement is provided, limiting reproducibility despite the benchmark and metric contributions.
There is no ethics/IRB discussion for the human-subject study, despite recruiting annotators via Prolific and compensating them.
Writing and citation issues (e.g., 'AHEAD' vs. 'AHEaD', 'HALucation', incorrect or malformed references) reduce clarity and suggest insufficient care in preparation.

strengths: Introduces CULTIVate, a novel benchmark focused on cross-cultural social activities rather than the object-centric categories dominant in prior cultural T2I evaluation.
Provides a substantial benchmark scale: 16 countries, 9 activity categories, 576 prompts, 19k+ generated images, 3k real reference images, and 6 recent T2I models.
Proposes explainable descriptor-based AHEaD metrics (Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, Diversity) with a proposer-refiner pipeline, enabling interpretable feedback beyond opaque VLM scores.

Human study includes nationality/residence constraints, attention checks, consistency checks, and fair compensation; the proposed FAITH metric shows stronger correlation with human faithfulness judgments than ITA baselines and MLLM judges.
Reports systematic Global North vs Global South bias across models, with complementary analysis of activity categories and descriptor dimensions.
Includes useful ablations on proposer-refiner and threshold calibration, and discusses limitations around LLM and real-image biases.
weaknesses: The central ground truth depends on LLM-generated descriptors and Google-searched real images filtered by CLIPScore; both may inherit cultural biases and are not guaranteed exhaustive or culturally authoritative. Human validation checks descriptor relevance (~90%) but not completeness or representativeness.

The exaggeration metric uses LLM-generated stereotype candidates and an unspecified image-text alignment score (likely CLIPScore), despite the paper criticizing CLIPScore for cultural evaluation. This may reintroduce the biases the paper aims to avoid.

FAITH is an unweighted arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, and 1-EXAG with no justification or ablation. Because EXAG is near ceiling, its scale may distort the composite; a learned or validated aggregation is missing.
Diversity metrics (DDIV, SDIV) are not validated against human judgments, even though diversity is a claimed contribution. No human annotation is collected for diversity.

Human evaluation is limited to 7 countries, 9 activities, 3 public models, and 216 forms; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Human-human agreement is moderate (0.42), and FAITH (0.38) is below it. The abstract/intro claim of '7% better correlation' is inconsistent with Table 2, which suggests a much larger improvement over baselines and needs correction.

Threshold tau is calibrated globally on noisy real images, and it is unclear whether it varies by country/activity. No sensitivity analysis is provided for the number of descriptors, descriptor dimensions, MLLM choice, or sentence embedding model.
Reproducibility is weak: there is no explicit code/data release statement for the benchmark or metrics, which is especially important for a benchmark contribution.

Model comparisons are not fully fair: proprietary models use N=1 due to cost while public models use N=10 for diversity, and the main ALIGN/HAL/EXAG table appears to mix N=1 settings, potentially understating public models' alignment at N=10.

Several writing and notation issues remain (e.g., 'CULTIVateBench' vs. 'CULTIVate', 'AHEaD' vs. 'AHEAD', equation notation, missing details on activity-country selection and exaggeration candidate generation), and no IRB/ethics statement is provided for the human study.

strengths: Introduces CULTIVate, a timely and useful benchmark for cultural faithfulness in text-to-image generation through social activities, covering 576 activities across 16 countries, 9 categories, 6 T2I models, and 19k+ generated images. It fills a gap left by prior object-centric cultural benchmarks (food, landmarks, attire).

Proposes AHEaD, an interpretable descriptor-based framework that decomposes cultural evaluation into Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, and Diversity. The use of proposer-refiner reference descriptors and MLLM-extracted predicted descriptors provides actionable diagnostics and avoids relying solely on VLM image-text alignment for cultural scoring.

Conducts a substantial human study across 11 countries with annotators matching each country's nationality, collecting ground-truth faithfulness, hallucination, exaggeration, and realism judgments. The paper compares against multiple ITA metrics, MLLM-as-judge baselines, and the cultural metric CuRe.

Provides convincing evidence that standard ITA metrics correlate poorly with human cultural faithfulness judgments (e.g., CLIPScore 0.04, ImageReward -0.08), and that combining alignment, hallucination, and exaggeration yields higher correlation than alignment alone.

Reveals systematic Global North vs. Global South disparities across all evaluated T2I models, supported by both automatic metrics and human judgments, and offers activity-level and descriptor-dimension analyses.

Includes useful ablations (proposer-refiner vs. proposer-only, threshold calibration) and detailed appendix prompts/implementation details that aid reproducibility. The preliminary descriptor-guided editing demonstration is promising, even if qualitative.
Addresses an important and understudied problem with broad relevance to cultural representation, creative content generation, and fairness in generative AI.
weaknesses: The central claim that FAITH achieves higher correlation than baselines is overstated. FAITH with InternVL3 reaches 0.47 Spearman correlation, which is slightly below the GPT-4o MLLM-as-judge baseline (0.48). The reported 27% improvement applies mainly to same-backbone MLLM judges, not to the strongest MLLM judge. The abstract/intro wording is ambiguous and should be corrected.

The Exaggeration metric is methodologically questionable. The paper argues ITA metrics are unreliable, yet EXAG uses VQAScore (an ITA metric) with LLM-generated stereotype candidates. The authors' own Table 9 shows MLLM-based EXAG has stronger correlation with human GT-EXAG (0.34) than the ITA-based EXAG used in FAITH (0.29). The choice of the weaker variant for interpretability weakens the composite metric.

The Exaggeration baseline is based on real images scraped from Google search and filtered by CLIPScore. These real images may themselves contain stereotypical or exaggerated content, so comparing generated images against them does not cleanly measure exaggeration. This risks circularity and cultural bias in the metric.

The Diversity components (DDIV, SDIV) are included in the AHEaD name but are not part of the FAITH composite and are not validated against human judgments of diversity. Their reliability and utility remain unclear, making the 'four dimensions' framing somewhat incomplete.

Human evaluation is relatively small: 398 forms / 796 annotations, only three public T2I models, and real images for three countries. Proprietary models are not human-evaluated. Inter-rater agreement is moderate (Krippendorff's alpha 0.15–0.62), so the ground truth itself is noisy. Absolute correlations around 0.47 are useful but leave substantial headroom.

Reference descriptors are LLM-generated and refined by GPT-4o, with no human-verified recall. The 90% precision and 4.5/5 coverage estimates are encouraging but do not guarantee that valid cultural variants are not missing. The benchmark activity lists are extracted from CulturalAtlas/Wikipedia via GPT-4o without reported human verification of coverage or representativeness.

Statistical support is incomplete: no confidence intervals or formal significance tests between competing metrics are reported, despite claims of 'significantly outperform'. The paper also contains typos and unclear details (e.g., missing standard deviations in Table 1, 'wcountries', 'exctractor'), and the descriptor-guided editing claim is supported only qualitatively without quantitative improvement evaluation.

strengths: Introduces CULTIVate, a new benchmark for cultural faithfulness in text-to-image generation through social activities, covering 16 countries, 576 activities, 9 categories, and over 19,000 generated images. This extends prior object-centric cultural benchmarks to more compositional and contextual social scenes.

Proposes AHEaD, a descriptor-based diagnostic framework that decomposes cultural evaluation into alignment, hallucination, exaggeration, and diversity. The descriptor-level feedback is interpretable and can support targeted image editing.
Conducts a human evaluation across 11 countries and 3 public T2I models, providing evidence that common image-text alignment metrics correlate poorly with human judgments of cultural faithfulness.

Shows that combining alignment with hallucination and exaggeration yields higher correlation with human faithfulness judgments than alignment alone, and reports systematic Global North vs. Global South disparities across six T2I models.
Includes useful ablations on proposer-refiner descriptor generation and threshold calibration, plus qualitative examples of descriptor-guided image refinement.
weaknesses: The central claim that FAITH achieves higher correlation than baselines is overstated. In Table 2, a simple GPT-4o MLLM-as-judge baseline obtains 0.48 overall correlation with human faithfulness, while FAITH obtains 0.47 with InternVL3 and 0.42 with Qwen2.5-VL. FAITH only outperforms weaker MLLM backbones, not the strongest baseline, yet the abstract and introduction imply broader superiority.

Reference descriptors are generated entirely by LLMs without guaranteed recall. The paper reports about 90% precision but only weakly estimates recall through a 4.5/5 coverage rating and 26/378 annotators reporting missing descriptors. Since alignment and hallucination metrics depend on this reference set, missing correct cultural elements can be incorrectly counted as hallucinations, undermining metric validity.

FAITH is an unweighted arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, and 1-EXAG, which are on incommensurate scales. EXAG is often very small (e.g., 0.05-0.12), making 1-EXAG near-constant and dominant in the average. This reduces sensitivity and makes the composite score hard to interpret.

The exaggeration metric relies on LLM-generated stereotype candidates and image-text alignment against real images. Its correlation with human exaggeration judgments is low (e.g., 0.183 average for stereotype candidates), and the paper adopts the lower-performing ITA variant for interpretability, further weakening FAITH.

The human evaluation is limited: 398 forms, 796 annotations, 11 countries, and only 3 public T2I models, with no human validation for proprietary models or the full 16-country benchmark. Inter-rater agreement is moderate (Krippendorff's alpha 0.15-0.62), and no confidence intervals or statistical tests for correlation differences are reported.

It is unclear whether ALIGN/HAL/EXAG/FAITH are computed with N=1 or N=10. Table 1 reports FAITH under an N=1 column even for public models where 10 images are generated, while diversity is reported under N=10. This inconsistency weakens cross-model comparisons and leaves the full framework under-evaluated.

Diversity metrics (DDIV and SDIV) are not validated against human judgments and are excluded from FAITH. The abstract claims AHEaD measures four dimensions, but only three contribute to the main faithfulness score, and diversity is not shown to be meaningful for cultural evaluation.

Benchmark construction relies on GPT-4o parsing CulturalAtlas and Wikipedia to extract activities, with no reported human verification of activity coverage or correctness. This raises concerns about noise and bias in the benchmark itself.

Reproducibility is insufficient. There is no mention of code or dataset release, and key implementation details are missing, including how descriptors are aggregated across images, how q(d) is computed for DDIV, the human study interface, and statistical treatment of nested annotations.

The writing and presentation contain duplicated paragraphs, ambiguous percentage-improvement claims, mangled references, and grammatical errors, which reduce clarity and make several claims difficult to verify.

strengths: Introduces CULTIVate, a novel and timely benchmark for evaluating cultural faithfulness of text-to-image models through social activities rather than object-centric artifacts. The benchmark spans 16 countries, 576 activities, 9 categories, and over 19k generated images, with 3k real reference images.

Proposes AHEaD, an interpretable descriptor-based framework that decomposes cultural evaluation into Alignment, Hallucination, Exaggeration, and Diversity. This provides diagnostic feedback beyond scalar scores and supports descriptor-guided image editing.

Conducts extensive experiments across 6 state-of-the-art T2I models and multiple baselines, including ITA metrics, MLLM-as-judge, and the cultural metric CuRe, with a human study covering 11 countries and 796 annotations.

Demonstrates convincingly that standard image-text alignment metrics correlate poorly with human judgments of cultural faithfulness, and that alignment alone is insufficient; the composite FAITH metric improves correlation over alignment-only and same-backbone MLLM baselines.
Reveals systematic Global North vs. Global South disparities, with generated images consistently more faithful for Global North cultures, and provides useful per-country and per-activity analyses.

Provides a preliminary but compelling demonstration that AHEaD's descriptor-level feedback can guide image editing to remove hallucinations and reduce exaggerated stereotypes, showing practical utility for iterative refinement.
Includes detailed implementation details, prompts, threshold calibration, and ablation studies, which support reproducibility and clarify design choices.

The human evaluation protocol includes quality controls such as nationality matching, attention checks, repeated questions, and free-text rationales, which strengthens the reliability of the annotation process.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction overstate the empirical results: FAITH with the best backbone (0.47) does not outperform the GPT-4o MLLM-as-judge baseline (0.48) in Table 2, yet the paper claims the highest correlation and '27% higher than baselines' without clearly restricting the comparison to same-backbone baselines. This overclaiming should be corrected.

The reference descriptors are entirely LLM-generated, so they may encode Western or stereotypical biases and may be incomplete. Human validation only measures precision (~90%) and self-reported coverage, not recall against a ground-truth descriptor set, so ALIGN and HAL could be systematically biased when valid cultural elements are missing from the reference set.

The real reference images used for threshold calibration and the EXAG metric are collected via Google search and filtered by CLIPScore—the very type of ITA metric the paper argues is culturally unreliable. This introduces potential bias into calibration and exaggeration baselines, weakening the methodological soundness of those components.

Human evaluation is limited to three public T2I models and 11 countries, with moderate inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's alpha 0.15–0.62). The noisy ground-truth labels may limit the strength of the correlation conclusions and the generalizability of the metric validation.

The FAITH composite is an unweighted arithmetic mean of ALIGN, 1-HAL, and 1-EXAG. The equal weighting and the assumption that these components are on comparable scales are not justified or ablated, leaving open whether a different combination would perform better.

The EXAG metric shows only modest correlation with human exaggeration judgments (e.g., 0.29), and it relies on LLM-generated stereotype candidates that are not human-validated. The paper notes that an MLLM-based EXAG variant correlates better but chooses the ITA-based version for interpretability, raising questions about the accuracy of the deployed exaggeration metric.
The diversity metrics (DDIV and SDIV) are not validated against human judgments and are excluded from FAITH, so their utility and relationship to cultural faithfulness remain unclear.

There is no clear statement that the CULTIVate benchmark, descriptors, code, or generated images will be publicly released. For a benchmark paper at a top-tier venue, reproducibility requires accessible resources.

The human annotation process includes direct discussions with annotators to resolve inconsistent scores, which may inadvertently bias the final labels. Additionally, compensation of $8/hour may be below fair wage in some annotator countries, raising minor ethical concerns.
